questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A coin is claimed to be fair. It landed heads 34 times in 50 flips. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 50 flips of a fair coin. Count runs with 34 or more heads. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.prompt_markup: A coin is claimed to be fair. It landed heads 34 times in 50 flips. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 50 flips of a fair coin. Count runs with 34 or more heads. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: 3 of 200 runs (1.5%) had 34 or more heads; 1.5% < 5%, so the data are evidence against a fair coin.
3 of 200 runs (1.5%) had 34 or more heads, so the coin is proved to be unfair.
A fair coin can never land heads 34 times in 50 flips, so the claim is false.
36 of 200 runs (18%) had 29 or more heads, so 34 heads is not unusual for a fair coin.

questions.correct_answer: 3 of 200 runs (1.5%) had 34 or more heads; 1.5% < 5%, so the data are evidence against a fair coin.
questions.grading_note: Only the ≥34 bar counts: 3/200. Evidence is not proof, and the event is rare, not impossible.

figure.description: Histogram (x-axis "Heads in 50 fair flips (200 simulated runs)", y-axis "Number of runs"). ≤19: 12, 20–22: 35, 23–25: 66, 26–28: 51, 29–31: 27, 32–33: 6, ≥34: 3.

data.xlabel: Heads in 50 fair flips (200 simulated runs)

questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A spinner is claimed to land on red 25% of the time. It landed on red 13 times in 40 spins. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 40 spins under the claim. Count runs with 13 or more reds. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.prompt_markup: A spinner is claimed to land on red 25% of the time. It landed on red 13 times in 40 spins. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 40 spins under the claim. Count runs with 13 or more reds. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: The expected count is 10, and 13 is not 10, so the claim is false.
34 of 200 runs (17%) had 13 or more reds, so the claim is proved true.
Only runs with exactly 13 reds count, which is rare, so the claim is rejected.
34 of 200 runs (17%) had 13 or more reds; 17% > 5%, so the result is consistent with the claim.

questions.correct_answer: 34 of 200 runs (17%) had 13 or more reds; 17% > 5%, so the result is consistent with the claim.
questions.grading_note: 20 + 14 = 34 runs. Consistent with the model does not prove it.

figure.description: Histogram (x-axis "Reds in 40 spins with P(red) = 0.25 (200 runs)", y-axis "Number of runs"). ≤4: 5, 5–6: 20, 7–8: 32, 9–10: 62, 11–12: 47, 13–14: 20, ≥15: 14.

data.xlabel: Reds in 40 spins with P(red) = 0.25 (200 runs)

questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A player claims to make 70% of her free throws. She made 11 of 20. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 20 shots under the claim. Count runs with 11 or fewer makes. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.prompt_markup: A player claims to make 70% of her free throws. She made 11 of 20. The histogram shows 200 simulated runs of 20 shots under the claim. Count runs with 11 or fewer makes. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: She made 11, not the expected 14, so the claim is false.
24 of 200 runs (12%) had 11 or fewer makes, so the 70% claim is proved true.
24 of 200 runs (12%) had 11 or fewer makes; 12% > 5%, so the result is consistent with the claim.
6 of 200 runs (3%) had 9 or fewer makes; 3% < 5%, so 11 makes is unusual.

questions.correct_answer: 24 of 200 runs (12%) had 11 or fewer makes; 12% > 5%, so the result is consistent with the claim.
questions.grading_note: 6 + 18 = 24 runs. Not unusual is not proof.

sections.skill: Compare two treatments with a re-randomization simulation

branch.new_demand: Apply the same model-testing logic to a randomized experiment.
branch.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the designed simulation for one proportion becomes a shuffle of treatment labels.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Compare two treatments with a re-randomization simulation
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: In an experiment, 20 plants were randomly assigned to fertilizer or no fertilizer, and the fertilized plants grew 2.9 cm more on average. The histogram shows 200 re-randomized differences under the model that fertilizer has no effect; none was 2.9 cm or more. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. What do you conclude?
questions.prompt_markup: In an experiment, 20 plants were randomly assigned to fertilizer or no fertilizer, and the fertilized plants grew 2.9 cm more on average. The histogram shows 200 re-randomized differences under the model that fertilizer has no effect; none was 2.9 cm or more. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. What do you conclude?

choices.text: 0/200 < 5%: a difference this large is very unlikely by chance, so fertilizer appears to increase growth.
The difference is not significant, because no re-randomized difference matched it exactly.
0/200: a difference this large has probability exactly 0, so the fertilizer is proved to work.
No conclusion is possible, because the result must first be compared with a fair coin.

questions.correct_answer: 0/200 < 5%: a difference this large is very unlikely by chance, so fertilizer appears to increase growth.
questions.grading_note: A rare result is evidence of an effect, not proof; probability is not shown to be zero.

choices.text: Both flip a real coin many times and then count how many heads appear in each of the groups of subjects in the study.
Both ask how often a model produces a result at least as extreme as the observed one; here the model is "no treatment effect."
The coin test uses a probability model, but the re-randomization test does not use any model of the results at all.
Both prove the model is true whenever the observed result turns out to be common among the simulated results.

questions.correct_answer: Both ask how often a model produces a result at least as extreme as the observed one; here the model is "no treatment effect."
questions.grading_note: Same logic, different null model. The others describe flipping a real coin, deny that re-randomization uses a model, or treat a common result as proof.
questions.set_target: Use supplied simulation results to decide whether a probability model is consistent with an observed result
questions.target_skill: Compare two treatments with a re-randomization simulation
